script.name: The big picture
script.narration: Proposition thirty-seven creates a loan program for buyers of qualifying new homes. The problem it targets is the upfront cash needed to buy, not the entire cost of housing. Assistance would be another loan, not free money. The state housing finance agency could issue up to twenty-five billion dollars in revenue bonds. Homebuyers’ payments would repay investors and administration. The analyst finds no direct state or local cost under this structure.

script.name: An illustrative example
script.narration: Imagine a family budgeting for a newly built home. For an illustrative home costing six hundred thousand dollars, three percent down is eighteen thousand dollars. A loan covering seventeen percent would be one hundred two thousand. The remaining eighty percent is four hundred eighty thousand. That can reduce cash needed at closing, but the family still owes the assistance loan as well as its main mortgage. Affordability depends on both monthly payments, interest rates, taxes, insurance, and other costs. The program is tied to qualifying new housing.

script.name: How it would work
script.narration: Borrowers must meet one year of California residency, owner-occupancy, and income rules, including an income ceiling tied to twice the area’s median. Homes must be qualifying first sales, with county-based price limits roughly around one million to one and a half million dollars, adjusted annually. How many loans could it fund? Using the example loan amount, the bond could support roughly two hundred and forty-five thousand loans. That is arithmetic, not an official forecast; actual loan sizes, issuance, and costs matter. Developers can build eligible homes without using the optional qualified-builder route. That option pairs higher labor standards with different construction-defect rules. The measure does not directly guarantee a particular number of homes will be built.

script.name: Why someone might vote yes
script.narration: A voter might support helping households with adequate income but too little saved cash. Restricting the assistance to new homes could encourage construction, connecting stronger purchasing power to additional supply. Whether developers respond enough is uncertain.

script.name: Why someone might vote no
script.narration: You might ask whether easier buying pushes prices up. If more buyers can bid while construction stays constrained, some benefit can be absorbed into higher prices. New-home eligibility helps link the program to supply, but does not remove land, labor, or permitting constraints. Easier financing alone is not a complete affordability solution. A skeptical voter could also question the extra household debt or the construction-defect tradeoff. No direct government cost does not mean every borrower benefits, or that every risk disappears.

script.name: What polling indicates
script.narration: In the September PPIC survey of likely voters, 61 percent said yes, 35 percent no, and 3 percent were unsure. These are dated survey results, not votes already cast.

script.name: Make your own decision
script.narration: Yes creates this loan program; no leaves existing assistance options in place without requiring the new program. Visit our website for the fuller explanation, source links, and official voter guide. Compare the tradeoffs, then make your own informed choice.
